readingInstruction: Read Luke 3:1-4:13. John preaches, Jesus is baptized and prays, a genealogy runs back to Adam, and the devil tests him in the wilderness. Compare this with Matthew’s accounts, and notice what Luke adds.
settingTheScene: Luke again places the story in history, naming Tiberius, Pilate, Herod, and the high priests. Into that world, the word of God comes to John in the wilderness. Luke’s account of John is fuller in some ways than Matthew’s, with specific advice for the crowds, tax collectors, and soldiers. His genealogy of Jesus runs backward to Adam rather than forward from Abraham, which fits Luke’s concern for all people.
observation: “The word of God came to John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness” (3:2).
“And all flesh shall see the salvation of God” (3:6).
“Whoever has two tunics is to share with him who has none, and whoever has food is to do likewise” (3:11).
“Now when all the people were baptized, and when Jesus also had been baptized and was praying, the heavens were opened” (3:21).
“The son of Adam, the son of God” (3:38).
“And Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit in the wilderness” (4:1).
“And when the devil had ended every temptation, he departed from him until an opportune time” (4:13).
interpretation:
Luke 3:6 quotes Isaiah 40 and goes a step further than the other Gospels, ending with “all flesh shall see the salvation of God.” This is Luke’s theme. John’s message is practical. When the crowds ask what to do, he tells them to share. Tax collectors are told to collect no more than they are authorized. Soldiers are to stop extorting. Repentance has a concrete shape: generosity and honesty.

At the baptism, Luke alone notes that Jesus was praying. This is the first of many times in Luke that prayer precedes a decisive moment in Jesus’ life. While he prays, the Spirit descends in bodily form and the Father speaks: “You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.” The Trinity is present: the Father speaks, the Son prays, and the Spirit descends.

The genealogy that follows runs from Jesus back through David, Abraham, Noah, and finally to Adam, “the son of God.” Jesus is the second Adam, and his story is humanity’s story. Where Adam failed in a garden, he will succeed in a wilderness.

In the temptation, Luke notes that Jesus was full of the Holy Spirit and led by the Spirit. He is hungry after forty days. The devil first tempts him to turn stones into bread, then offers him all the kingdoms of the world, and finally takes him to the pinnacle of the temple and quotes Scripture to him. Jesus answers each time with a verse from Deuteronomy. Luke reverses the order of the second and third temptations from Matthew, ending in Jerusalem, where the story will end. The devil departs “until an opportune time,” a hint that the real battle is still ahead.

The Son of God does not use his power to serve himself. He relies on the word of God and the Spirit, as we must.
connection: Isaiah 40:3-5 is the passage John fulfills. Genesis 3 is the first temptation, and Romans 5:12-19 contrasts Adam and Christ. 1 Corinthians 15:45 calls Christ the last Adam. Hebrews 2:18 says that because he himself has suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted. Luke 22:3 shows the devil’s return at the “opportune time,” when Satan enters Judas. Ephesians 6:17 describes the sword of the Spirit.
application:
Ask what fruit in keeping with repentance would look like for you this week. Be as practical as John was.

When temptation comes, answer it with Scripture, as Jesus did. Choose a verse to carry.

Pray before big decisions, as Jesus did at his baptism.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus, the last Adam, for resisting where the first fell.
Ask him to fill you with his Spirit.
Tell him where you are being tempted.
